P1.evidence: No setter suffix on the title and no application referenced, so P1a does not apply. The frame ran with the disqualification clause included: 'go into where you're currently at, where you want to go, see if we can help you bridge that gap. If we can, I will take a little bit through how. If I feel like we're not the best fit, perfectly fine. I'll point you in the right direction, okay?' — three parts, with 'what's in the way' and 'what you need' absent. Agreement was sought with the trailing 'okay?' and given ('Perfect'). The open question ran.

P2.evidence: Split sharply between what the rep asked well and what he never touched. Excellent on the training picture: current frequency and the cut from five days to three, the specific plateau numbers on pull-ups and bench, and a 1-to-10 scale on the back pain that established it as persistent and varying between 4 and 6. Diet was covered properly — composition, protein frequency, cheat meals, processed food, alcohol. Age, height and weight were all asked, though not until 00:12:12. But the rep never once asked what the prospect does for a living; the shift pattern only surfaced incidentally while discussing meal timing, which left the single most important ICP criterion unassessable. Health conditions were never asked either — SIBO was volunteered during the nutrition discussion and never followed up. Sleep was never raised despite the prospect working occasional 11pm-to-7am shifts, and daily energy was never asked.

P3.evidence: The surface and middle layers were run properly. The 'something you want to do but can't' question ran explicitly — 'Do you have like an example of something that you would like to be able to do which is now not 100% possible?' — and it was the most productive question in the call, surfacing Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu and indoor climbing, both deferred because of the back. The bridge question ran twice, once bare and once with examples, but produced nothing: 'I haven't thought about it. Not really.' The impact question ran on both the pain and the hobbies. Where it failed is the final drive: 'who else does that impact?' was never asked, no family, partner or relationships were explored at any point, and the deep why never went past 'more challenging' and personal confidence. The closing recap was accurate and confirmed but stayed a list of physical targets rather than the 'this isn't really about the weight' reframe.

P4.evidence: Asked properly and repeatedly, but the prospect had little to give. 'Outside of kettlebells, have you tried anything other than working out?' ran and returned 'no, I just did the gym'. The rep pushed on why he had not acted sooner more than once — 'what stopped you from already trying something else out prior to this?' and later 'what then sort of came up for you to not go there yet?' — and got 'I don't know, I don't have an answer for that' both times, which is a fair hit for asking. The gap was named by the prospect himself in response to a direct question: form correction and structure around food, not training discipline. The previous personal trainer at 200 euros a month was volunteered late and never explored — what happened, why it ended, what it did or did not fix, all unasked. The most relevant scripted question of the whole phase went unused: this is a man who never misses a session but has no food structure, and 'the information isn't the problem, why can't you stick to it on your own?' was never put to him.

P5.evidence: The two-year projection ran and, to the rep's credit, he noticed the prospect had misunderstood it as 'what would you do instead' and rephrased it: 'if you just stick to doing three workouts a week you don't make changes at all... what do you feel like it would look like?' The settle question ran cleanly and got a real answer — 'no, I mean, I wouldn't be happy. I would want to make the change.' But 'why not?' was asserted back at the prospect rather than asked of him, and the line-in-the-sand question was never put. Note for the flags rather than the score: the consequence the rep chose to make vivid was that the prospect might have to see a doctor or take medication for his back, which is an odd thing to frame as the bad outcome for an undiagnosed multi-year pain.

P6.evidence: The belief question ran before the presentation, correctly placed: 'do you feel like you're going to be able to follow through with that if we actually get started?' — answered 'yeah, I think I will be able to follow his instructions.' A 1-to-10 scale question was then run after the presentation but before price, which is a reasonable substitute for the all-in check and returned a 10. But the scripted isolation question — 'if you had everything you needed, is there any reason you wouldn't go all in?' — was never asked in that form, and this is where the call was lost. Had it been asked, the local clinic the prospect had already been considering would almost certainly have surfaced before the number rather than four minutes after it.

P11.evidence: A close was attempted and price was presented, but the prospect declined outright and never agreed to proceed, so none of the four payment and onboarding steps were reachable. Scored not applicable rather than miss so that a clean, well-handled loss is not penalised for steps that only exist after a yes.

objection_plays.detail: The rep believed the trigger was present and opened the play on it — 'Sounds like that's more like a money thing, right?' — but the diagnosis was wrong, and the prospect corrected it within two minutes: 'I could spend it, I have to save. I have that money saved.' Of the scripted moves, only the hypothetical and a vague willingness to structure ran: 'we can always figure something out to actually make it work... if it's just too much to pay all in one go.' No isolation question, no HOW-versus-SHOULD reframe, and none of the six financial-picture questions — which was correct, since capacity was never the issue. Graded partial because the play was opened and half-run on a trigger that was not actually there; the real cost is that four minutes were spent on money while the value objection went unaddressed.

The fear and doubt trigger was explicit and the prospect said the quiet part out loud: 'is it worth spending it if you don't really know how it's, how the outcome is going to be?' That is textbook certainty-seeking and OE exists precisely for it. None of it ran — no 'would it be fair to say you're looking for certainty?', no pleasure-versus-pain question, no bridge, no plane analogy, no 'how will you know if you never actually try?'. Compounding it, no guarantee, refund or risk reversal was mentioned anywhere in the call, so the prospect's stated need for outcome certainty was met with nothing at all.

Script gap, and a sharper version of the one already logged in the playbook. The known gap describes 'a cheaper alternative already worked for me'; here the alternative is not cheaper but priced at parity — roughly 6K over a year at a local clinic with doctors, physiotherapists and personal trainers he can see face to face, with social proof from people he knows personally. The playbook has no play for an equal-priced, higher-trust, in-person competitor, so the rep improvised: a sustainability reframe, which was reasonable and the strongest move he made, followed by a story disparaging such clinics as financially motivated. The prospect did not move. Worth escalating as a product and positioning question rather than a rep failure — remote delivery genuinely does not do what he was buying.

notes: Discovery was the best in this batch on the training and pain picture, and the rep persisted intelligently when questions were misunderstood. Two failures decided it. He never asked what the prospect does for work, which left affordability and ICP unassessable and led him to spend the critical minutes after price running a money play against an objection that was about value. And he skipped the all-in isolation question before presenting, so a competing option the prospect had already been weighing surfaced only after the number. Coach on isolating before price, and on treating 'I don't know if it will work' as the fear play rather than as a money signal.
